title: Learning Pronunciations
subtitle: The Science of Sound
summary: The fifty mother sounds, where each one is formed in the mouth, and why the difference matters.

quote.text: The Vedas come from certain fundamental sounds, and their variations. The slightest modification of the sound changes the meaning.

blocks.heading: Mantras are vibrations
blocks.intro: A sound does not begin at the lips. It rises through four levels before it is heard.

blocks.heading: Sound perfection: step one
blocks.iast: oṃ yad-akṣara¹ pada² bhraṣṭaṃ mātrā³hīnantu yadbhavet | tat sarvaṃ kṣamyatān deva nārāyaṇa namostute ||

notes.meaning: combination of those sounds as in a word
duration, or time taken to utter the sounds

blocks.heading: The fifty mother sounds
blocks.intro: Mātṛika, or varṇa. Fourteen need no aid — the vowels. Thirty-six are formed with aid — the consonants. Every one belongs to a place in the mouth. Choose a place to see its sounds.
footnotes: Short vowels take one unit of time; long vowels take two.
The combination vowels are built from the simple ones: e = a + i, o = a + u, ai = a + ī, au = a + ū.
Fourteen vowels in all, and twenty-eight of the thirty-six consonants sit in these five places.

blocks.heading: The force of chanting
blocks.intro: Each varga pairs an unaspirated sound with an aspirated one. The aspirated sound carries a push of breath, and losing it changes the word.

blocks.heading: Practice
blocks.intro: Words drawn from the chants, each turning on a vowel you have just met.

source: Vedas4All — VedaStudy: The Science of Sound, module 1

title: Continuity — Anusvāra
subtitle: The Science of Sound
summary: The dot that is never itself. How ṁ takes the colour of whatever sound follows it, and why chanting flows because of it.

blocks.heading: Where we left off
blocks.intro: Module 1 laid out the fifty mother sounds and gave every one of them a place in the mouth. Those same five places are what this module turns on.

stats.label: Places: guttural, palatal, cerebral, dental, labial

blocks.heading: This module: the dot
blocks.intro: *Anusvāra* is the **bindu** — the dot. In IAST it is written ṁ; in Devanāgarī it is a dot placed above the letter. It is a nasal sound, and on its own it has no fixed identity.
items: The dot is not a letter you pronounce the same way every time.
What it becomes is decided entirely by the sound that comes **after** it.
Getting this right is what makes chanting continuous rather than a string of separate words.

blocks.heading: When ṁ meets a consonant
blocks.intro: When an ṁ meets a consonant it changes into a nasal sound according to the place of articulation, specific for each group of consonants. The nasal sounds are pronounced like the other consonants at the same place, using the tongue in the same position — but the sound comes out through the nose instead of the mouth.

groups.label: Palatal
groups.note: Several examples run all through the Camakam.

blocks.heading: When ṁ meets a semivowel
blocks.intro: Before y, l and v the dot does not become a nasal consonant. It keeps its own nasal hum and carries a trace of the following sound into it.

blocks.heading: The gṁ sound
blocks.intro: Before a sibilant, the dot hardens into a distinct **gṁ**.

blocks.heading: The g and gg sounds
blocks.intro: Which one you get depends on the length of the vowel before the dot.
footnotes: **Long** vowel followed by ṁ (or n) + sibilant + consonant or semi-consonant gives **g**.
**Short** vowel followed by ṁ (or n) + sibilant + consonant or semi-consonant gives **gg**.

blocks.heading: Complete anusvāra
blocks.intro: In a *bījākṣara* — a seed syllable — the dot is not modified by anything. It stays a pure ṁ.
items: oṁ, and the other bījākṣara.
oṁ | namo bhagavate
saṁjñānam

blocks.heading: Summary
items: Before a **consonant** — the dot becomes that place's **nasal**: ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma.
Before a **semivowel** — it carries a trace vowel: **i** before y, **l** before l, **u** before v.
Before a **sibilant** — it hardens: **gṁ**, **g**, or **gg**.
In a **bījākṣara** — it stays a pure **ṁ**, unchanged.

source: Learning Continuity (Anusvāra) — VedaStudy, The Science of Sound

title: Continuity — Visarga
subtitle: The Science of Sound
summary: The breath that is sent forth. How ḥ is pronounced, reshaped, or dropped altogether depending on what follows it.

blocks.heading: This module: the visarga
blocks.intro: *Visarga* means **that which is discharged, or sent forth**. In IAST it is written as an h with a dot below. In Devanāgarī it is two dots beside a letter.
items: Like the anusvāra, the visarga rarely stays as itself.
What follows it decides whether it is pronounced, changed into another sound, or dropped.

blocks.heading: Visarga before a consonant
blocks.intro: Each place of articulation reshapes the visarga into its own sibilant.

groups.label: Guttural
groups.note: The visarga is not lost here — it is held as a breath before the k.

examples.text: vāja̍śca me prasa̱vaśca̍ me̱ praya̍tiśca me̱ prasi̍tiśca me

groups.label: Before a sibilant
groups.note: The visarga simply takes the shape of the sibilant that follows.

blocks.heading: aḥ becomes o
blocks.intro: Visarga preceded by **a** becomes **o** when it is followed by a vowel *a*, by *y, r, l, v*, by *h*, or by any of the soft consonants.
footnotes: The soft consonants in full: g, gh, ṅ · j, jh, ñ · ḍ, ḍh, ṇ · d, dh, n · b, bh, m.

blocks.heading: aḥ becomes a
blocks.intro: Visarga preceded by **a** becomes plain **a** when it is followed by any vowel **except** *a*.

blocks.heading: Visarga after other vowels
blocks.intro: After i, u and ū the visarga echoes its own vowel before joining what follows.

blocks.heading: The h reversal
blocks.intro: Where an **h** is followed by a nasal, the two swap in the mouth — the nasal is sounded first.
footnotes: No change if the h is followed by **y, r, l** or **v** — for example *prahlāda*.

blocks.heading: Summary
items: Visarga and bindu are **critical for continuity** in chanting.
Visarga gets pronounced, modified, or even omitted depending on the vowels or consonants that follow it.
Careful attention has to be paid to avoid discontinuities — both within words and in the linkages between them.
There are many more nuances to these changes than are covered here.

source: Learning Continuity (Visarga) — VedaStudy, The Science of Sound

title: Discontinuity — Pauses & Holdings
subtitle: The Science of Sound
summary: Where to stop, where never to stop, and how long to hold a sound — what keeps a group chanting as one voice.

blocks.heading: This module
blocks.intro: So far we have covered purpose, meter (*chandas*), sounds (*varṇa*), duration (*mātra*), and continuity — visarga and bindu — both **within** words (*pada*) and **between** them (*pāda*).
items: Pauses.
Holdings.
Focusing on syllables, with śloka examples.
Attention to common flaws in chanting.

blocks.heading: Pauses
blocks.intro: The written marks tell you where a line ends. The rest you have to hear.

items.label: Single vertical line ।
examples: yā ta̱ | iṣuś śi̱vatamā śi̱vam ba̱bhūva te̱ dhanuḥ ।

items.label: Double vertical line ॥
items.text: Indicates completion of the śloka or mantra — ṛk or yajus.
examples: śivā śaravyā yā tava tayā no rudra mṛḍaya ॥

items.label: Short pause
items.text: Between two words, where the first ends and the second begins with short vowels.
examples: yā ta | iṣuś śi̱vatamā śi̱vam ba̱bhūva te̱ dhanuḥ ।

items.label: One unit time pause
items.text: When a word ends with a long vowel and the next starts with a short vowel.
examples: yo ru̱dro | a̱gnau yo | a̱psu ya | oṣa̍dhīṣu̱

blocks.heading: Pauses within words

items.label: Pause ḥ:a
items.text: When a visarga is followed by a compounded consonant such as *kṣa*.

items.label: Short pause within a word
items.text: When an anusvāra is followed by a compounded consonant.

items.label: Short pause after oṁ
items.text: After chanting oṁ or a bījākṣara.

items.label: Short pause at a half-consonant
items.text: When a word ends with a half-consonant within a line.

footnotes: Overall, pauses help with **breath management** during chanting.

blocks.heading: Breaks not allowed
blocks.intro: Some places look like a pause and are not. Breaking here changes the meaning.

items.label: At an avagraha
items.text: Marked ' in IAST, or ऽ in Devanāgarī. **A break at the avagraha distorts the meaning.**

items.label: At a conjunction with visarga or anusvāra
items.text: Shown by the blue letters in the chant documents — the sound carries straight through.

blocks.heading: Holdings
blocks.intro: Holding the sounds — *akṣara* — is what gives a group its **timing and synchronicity**. A short holding follows a short vowel, marked as a thin rectangle in IAST and a single ͂ in Devanāgarī. A long holding follows a long vowel, marked as a thick rectangle, or ͌ in Devanāgarī.

items.alt: yāmiṣuṅ giriśanta haste bibharṣyastave, with thin rectangles marking short holdings
items.caption: Short holding — the thin rectangles

items.alt: The same line in Devanāgarī, with single marks above the syllables
śivāṅ giritra tāṅ kuru mā hiṁgṁsīḥ puruṣañ jagat, with thick rectangles marking long holdings
items.caption: Long holding — the thick rectangles

items.alt: The same line in Devanāgarī, with double marks above the syllables

footnotes: These marks have no character of their own in the fonts, so they are shown here exactly as they appear in the teaching deck.

blocks.heading: Counting syllables
blocks.intro: Sixteen syllables — **Anuṣṭup chandas**. The green boxes mark the syllables; the blue superscripts are the anusvāra changes from Module 2, carried into a real verse.

items.alt: śuklām baradharaṁ viṣṇuṁ śaśi varṇañ caturbhujam | prasanna vadanan dhyāyet sarva vighno-paśāntaye ||, with each syllable boxed
items.caption: śuklām baradharaṁ viṣṇuṁ śaśi varṇañ caturbhujam ॥

footnotes: The first line has 15 short and 1 long syllable. At 0.17 seconds for a short syllable and 2.5 for a long one, that is about **5 seconds**.
The second line has 12 short and 4 long syllables — about **12 seconds**.

blocks.heading: A second example
blocks.intro: Sixteen syllables again, Anuṣṭup chandas. The eighth syllable in each line has a long vowel, which creates a pause pattern.
footnotes: **This is not a rhythm.** One has to pay attention to the short vowels and not pause there.

items.label: Singing
items.text: The Vedas have explicit *svara* and should be chanted accordingly.

items.label: Too fast
items.text: Too fast is incorrect. Practise at lower speed. Listen and experience the total vibration — pronunciation, intonation, duration, force, consistency, and continuity.

items.label: Shaking the head, and the whole body
items.text: Use hand movement if needed for the svaras. Not the whole body.

items.label: Reading from a book
items.text: This is a tough one. Memorise and chant by heart. Remember: **HE + ART = HEART**.

items.label: Chanting without understanding the meaning
items.text: At least make an earnest effort to study the mantra and its application to self-transformation.

source: Discontinuity — Pauses / Holdings — VedaStudy, The Science of Sound
